source_text: ex Adam nihil mali transisse per ceteros nisi mortem, quae non semper est malum, inquiunt, cum et martyribus sit causa praemiorum et vel bonam vel malam mortem dici faciat non resolutio corporum, quae in omni hominum genere resuscitabitur, sed meritorum differentia, quae de humana libertate descendit
pass_a_gloss: that from Adam nothing evil has passed through the rest except death, which is not always an evil, they say, since for martyrs it is a cause of rewards, and what makes death called good or evil is not the dissolving of bodies, which will be raised in every kind of human beings, but the difference of deserts, which descends from human freedom

lemmas.lexica: LS malum; Blaise malum naturale vs malum voluntatis
LS meritum=desert; Blaise without later merit-system
LS libertas; Blaise moral freedom to will or refuse

pass_b_english: Nothing evil has passed from Adam to everyone else except death (Romans 5:12). Death is not always an evil, since for martyrs it is a cause of rewards. What makes death good or bad is not the dissolution of bodies, which will be raised in every class of human beings (possible echo: John 5:28–29), but the difference in people’s deserts, which arises from human freedom.

choices.why: Glossary: avoid modern merit-theology; Julian means deserved outcome.
Freedom to abstain is required for will and sin.

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded. Julian is not first-English.

speaker: Julian and fellow bishops (Collective letter to Thessalonica, words preserved in Augustine, Contra duas epistolas Pelagianorum 2–4); Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded.
kind: quotation preserved partly in indirect speech
